title: Government Doesn't Just Waste Your Money — It Wastes an Hour of Your Week
dek: Plenty of countries file taxes for their citizens; the IRS is legally barred from doing it for you. The time tax hits the poor, immigrants and the formerly incarcerated hardest — and AI may not save them.
why: Medium information density, but the "time tax" framing itself is valuable: it reprices the administrative friction of the welfare state as a kind of regressive levy. The back half, where she admits her UBI priors have shifted, is worth hearing.
who: People working in public policy, government digital services or benefits products; engineers wondering whether AI can replace administrative processes; and readers who want to understand why the American welfare state is so inefficient.
skip: The 36:25 to 38:28 argument about how easy voting is — both sides talk past each other, low information gain.

points.h: The IRS is legally barred from filing your taxes for you
points.body: Lowrey's central example: in Japan, salaried workers never touch the tax process at all; many countries mail you a pre-filled return and you just correct the errors. The US could easily do the same — nine in ten households take the standard deduction, and their tax situations are fairly simple — but the IRS is not legally permitted to. This isn't a technology problem, it's an institutional choice. She defines the "time tax" as the portion of cost the government shifts onto individuals as administrative labour, and unlike a monetary tax it's different in kind: you can earn more money, you can't earn more time.

points.h: The worst program is TANF, not the IRS
points.body: Lowrey names TANF (cash welfare) the single worst program in government: it nominally exists to address child poverty, in practice it doesn't move the child poverty rate, its compliance requirements are extremely onerous and punitive, and its $16.5 billion a year is essentially wasted. She offers a rule — programs aimed at high-income Americans are a far better experience, safety-net programs are generally bad, and welfare is the worst. That yields a counterintuitive judgment: the quality of government service is inversely proportional to the political power of its recipients.

points.h: Pandemic fraud isn't something the time tax can prevent
points.body: Cowen raises a common objection: fraud exploded after deregulation in 2020, so maybe the time tax is just the necessary cost of fraud prevention. Lowrey rejects it outright: that fraud came mainly from criminal rings and fake small businesses, plus the fact that UI systems themselves run on ancient COBOL infrastructure. Her mechanism is misaligned incentives — governors have no incentive to upgrade UI systems when unemployment is low, so the same conversation repeats every recession. The conclusion: building state capacity and agile digital systems prevents fraud; pushing the work onto individuals does not.

points.h: Large-scale fraud is almost entirely on the supply side
points.body: Lowrey points out that Medicare and Medicaid fraud is almost entirely on the provider side: nursing homes, clinics and hospital systems defrauding the government. The ceiling on individual fraud is low, because there's only so much money you can get from the government; to commit large-scale fraud you have to process a lot of transactions. So her policy ordering is: reduce administrative overhead in other programs, concentrate enforcement resources on criminal organisations and legitimate providers, rather than loading burdens onto the 99.9% who don't commit fraud. She adds a piece of political economy: fraud narratives are often used to make programs look illegitimate, which lets voters tolerate cuts.

points.h: Fifty hours a year each, and highly unequal
points.body: Lowrey's quantitative estimate comes from the American Time Use Survey: total bureaucratic time is about 50 hours per person per year, close to an hour a week. She concedes the number is understated — ATUS can't capture multitasking (cooking while on hold gets recorded as one activity), and time taxes are scattered across categories and never aggregated. Who pays the most? People entangled with the criminal justice system, immigrants, the poor. The rich can "skip the line" with staff and accountants — with one exception: permits to renovate a house in San Francisco, where no amount of money spares you a 500-day wait and multiple rounds of public review.

points.h: AI can fill out forms, but it can't fill a urine test
points.body: Cowen asks whether AI agents could handle all of this within five years. Lowrey says probably, but raises two caveats: first, the users of the most onerous programs are low-income, and whether they know about or trust these agents is an open question; second, much of the burden isn't paperwork at all — it's mandatory interviews, urine screening, data that's hard to collect. She gives SNAP as an example: benefits are calculated by household, and the government has no stable definition of "household", so you have to explain how you and your co-residents split food costs — the kind of question AI struggles to answer for you too. She notes she was originally sceptical, but a civic technologist who has worked in this field for years is convinced AI will help enormously.

points.h: Disability insurance is already hard enough to apply for
points.body: Cowen presses with data: the number of people on disability insurance rose roughly fourfold between 1990 and 2014, while workplace fatalities kept falling — shouldn't the threshold be raised? Lowrey doesn't accept the inference. She offers two alternative explanations: population ageing and rising obesity-related chronic illness. Then the counter-evidence: 5% of applicants have to submit more than 1,000 pages of medical material; 11,000 Americans die each year while waiting for a disability determination. She admits she worries about both directions — about paying people who don't need it, and about denying people who do — so she doesn't think this is the moment to add more paperwork.

points.h: Her UBI position was shaken by the research
points.body: Lowrey's previous book, Give People Money, was pro-UBI; here she says plainly that the research findings are "sobering" and that she has updated her priors: the knock-on benefits she expected cash to deliver didn't materialise. But her defence is that the point of giving people money is to give people money to buy things, and that rationale still holds; life improving less than expected isn't an argument against the policy. On AI and UBI, she admits she was extremely dismissive back then of the claim that "AI will force UBI", and she won't go that far now — but if GDP and productivity surge while unemployment rises at the same time, that would be very strange, and you'd have to start considering UBI-type policies.

terms.def: The time cost imposed on individuals when government shifts administrative labour onto them; unlike a monetary tax, it can't be offset by earning more.
Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, the US cash welfare program; Lowrey considers it the most administratively burdensome and least effective program in government.
Benefits delivered through the tax code that recipients often don't realise they're receiving, such as the child tax credit.
Efficiency gains increase total consumption rather than reducing it; Lowrey uses it to explain how labour-saving tools like email ended up adding to the task load.
An erroneous payment caused by complex rules, distinct from deliberate fraud, and reducible simply by simplifying the rules.
